senses.gloss: Not moving around or getting any exercise.
examples: Sitting at a desk all day leaves you *inactive* for hours at a time.
*Inactive* dogs put on weight fast.
He is even more *inactive* now than he was last winter.

senses.gloss: Not working, not in use, or no longer taking part.
examples: Your account has been *inactive* for six months.
The volcano has been *inactive* since 1957.

contrast: A false friend. Russian «неадекватный» usually means unreasonable or out of control; English *inadequate* means not enough or not good enough.

senses.gloss: Not enough, or not good enough for what is needed.
examples: The funding is *inadequate* for a school this size.
Our old wiring proved *inadequate*.
The second plan was even more *inadequate* than the first.

senses.gloss: Feeling that you are not good enough.
examples: Her comments made me feel *inadequate*.
He always felt *inadequate* next to his older brother.

senses.gloss: Not allowed to be used, especially as evidence in a court.
examples: The judge ruled the confession *inadmissible*.
*Inadmissible* evidence never reaches the jury.
Anything found in that search is legally *inadmissible*.

senses.gloss: Done by accident, without meaning to.
examples: One *inadvertent* click sent the email to the whole company.
The damage was *inadvertent*, but it was still expensive.
Most of these errors are *inadvertent*.

contrast: Almost always with *right* or *rights*. The Declaration of Independence spells it *unalienable*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to someone in a way that cannot be taken away.
examples: Voting is an *inalienable* right of every citizen.
The treaty speaks of the *inalienable* rights of every people.
They regard clean water as an *inalienable* right.

senses.gloss: Silly and completely without meaning.
examples: He made some *inane* comment about my haircut.
The questions got more *inane* as the interview went on.
I can't sit through another hour of *inane* chatter.

contrast: Grammar uses the word too: an *inanimate* noun takes *it*, not *he* or *she*.

senses.gloss: Not alive; not a living creature.
examples: A rock is an *inanimate* object.
Small children talk to *inanimate* things all the time.
In that painting even the furniture hardly looks *inanimate*.

senses.gloss: Not right for the occasion, the person or the place.
examples: That joke was *inappropriate* for a work meeting.
She wore shoes that were completely *inappropriate* for a hike.
Nothing could be more *inappropriate* than laughing at a funeral.

senses.gloss: Unable to say clearly what you mean, or not said clearly.
examples: He gets *inarticulate* when he is nervous.
Her answer was an *inarticulate* mumble.
I felt more *inarticulate* with every question they asked.

senses.gloss: Not watching or listening carefully enough.
examples: The waiter was friendly but *inattentive*.
*Inattentive* drivers cause most of these crashes.
He grew more *inattentive* as the lecture went on.

senses.gloss: Too quiet to be heard.
examples: His voice was almost *inaudible* over the traffic.
She muttered an *inaudible* reply.
The last word on the recording is *inaudible*.

contrast: Also a noun: *the inaugural* is the ceremony itself.

senses.gloss: First of its kind, or marking the start of something.
examples: She gave her *inaugural* speech on a freezing January morning.
The team plays its *inaugural* game in April.
This is the festival's *inaugural* year.

senses.gloss: Suggesting that what follows will go badly.
examples: It was an *inauspicious* start to the season.
The weather on opening day was *inauspicious*.
Few debuts have been more *inauspicious* than his.

senses.gloss: Present in a person from birth rather than learned.
examples: She has an *inborn* sense of rhythm.
*Inborn* errors of metabolism show up in newborns.
His caution seems *inborn* rather than taught.

senses.gloss: Coming in toward a place, rather than leaving it.
examples: All *inbound* flights are delayed by the storm.
*Inbound* traffic on the bridge is backed up for miles.
The train is *inbound* from Newark.

senses.gloss: Bred from parents that are close relatives.
examples: The herd is badly *inbred*.
*Inbred* mice are standard in lab research.

senses.gloss: Deep in someone since childhood, almost part of their nature.
examples: He has an *inbred* distrust of banks.
Her politeness is *inbred*.

senses.gloss: Too great or too complicated to be measured.
examples: The storm did *incalculable* damage to the coast.
The value of her work to this lab is *incalculable*.
War causes *incalculable* human suffering.

contrast: *Incandescent with rage* (furious) is mainly British; Americans say *livid*.

senses.gloss: Giving off light because it is heated until it glows.
examples: Old *incandescent* bulbs waste most of their energy as heat.
The steel came out of the furnace white and *incandescent*.
He replaced every *incandescent* fixture with LEDs.

contrast: *Incapable of doing* — never *incapable to do*. It is *unable* that takes the *to*-infinitive.

senses.gloss: Not able to do something at all.
examples: He is *incapable* of lying.
The old engine is *incapable* of pulling that load.
She seemed *incapable* of sitting still for a minute.

senses.gloss: Unable to act or function normally, usually through injury or illness.
examples: He was *incapacitated* by a back injury for three months.
The crash left the pilot *incapacitated*.
If the president is *incapacitated*, the vice president takes over.

contrast: Formal, and standard in American news writing: *incarcerated people* rather than *inmates*.

senses.gloss: Held in a prison or jail.
examples: He has been *incarcerated* since 2019.
The program helps *incarcerated* men finish high school.
Her brother is *incarcerated* in a federal prison in Kentucky.

contrast: Also a noun: *an incendiary* is a fire bomb, or a person who stirs up trouble.

senses.gloss: Made to start a fire.
examples: *Incendiary* bombs destroyed most of the old city.
The fire was set with a homemade *incendiary* device.

senses.gloss: Likely to stir up anger or violence.
examples: His speech was deliberately *incendiary*.
The article made some *incendiary* claims about the mayor.
Nothing he wrote was more *incendiary* than that last paragraph.

form: in- + a Latin form of *cease* — literally *not ceasing*

senses.gloss: Going on and on without stopping.
examples: The *incessant* barking next door kept me up all night.
We worked through two days of *incessant* rain.
Her questions were *incessant*.

senses.gloss: Involving sex between close relatives.
examples: The novel deals with an *incestuous* relationship.
*Incestuous* marriage is illegal in every state.

senses.gloss: So closed that the same small group deals only with itself.
examples: The city's political scene is famously *incestuous*.
Publishing can feel like an *incestuous* little world.
No industry is more *incestuous* than this one.

contrast: *Incidental music* is the background music of a play or film. The adverb *incidentally* means 'by the way'.

senses.gloss: Happening alongside something more important; minor.
examples: The grant covers travel, meals and *incidental* costs.
The damage to the fence was *incidental*.
Those details are *incidental* to the main argument.

senses.gloss: Getting straight to the heart of a matter, in a clear and sharp way.
examples: She asked two *incisive* questions and the whole case fell apart.
His commentary is *incisive* without being cruel.
The second essay is far more *incisive* than the first.

contrast: Used almost only of weather, and mostly in announcements and official notices.

senses.gloss: Cold, wet or stormy.
examples: The game was called off because of *inclement* weather.
In *inclement* conditions the ferry does not run.
The school has an *inclement* weather policy for buses.

position: both — the *inclined to* senses after a verb, the sloping sense before a noun

senses.gloss: Feeling that you want to do something, or likely to do it.
examples: I am *inclined* to agree with her.
He is *inclined* to exaggerate when he tells that story.
After the review, I am more *inclined* to wait a year.

senses.gloss: Having a natural talent for or interest in something.
examples: Their daughter is musically *inclined*.
The class is for students who are more technically *inclined*.

senses.gloss: Sloping rather than flat or upright.
examples: We studied the *inclined* plane in physics.
The roof is steeply *inclined*.

contrast: In dates and page ranges it follows the noun: *Monday through Friday inclusive*.

senses.gloss: Deliberately open to everyone, leaving no group out.
examples: The new hiring policy is meant to be more *inclusive*.
She runs an *inclusive* classroom where nobody sits alone.
It is the most *inclusive* club on campus.

senses.gloss: Containing everything mentioned, with nothing charged on top.
examples: The price is *inclusive* of tax and tips.
The course runs June 3 to June 14 *inclusive*.

contrast: More often an adverb: *she travels incognito*. As an adjective it only follows a verb — never *an incognito actor*.

senses.gloss: Hiding who you really are, usually under another name.
examples: The singer was *incognito* in a baseball cap and sunglasses.
For two weeks he stayed *incognito* in a small hotel.
She prefers to remain *incognito* at these events.

senses.gloss: Not making sense, because the parts do not hang together.
examples: He was so tired that he was *incoherent* by midnight.
The letter is an *incoherent* mix of complaints and threats.
Their energy policy is more *incoherent* than it was a year ago.

senses.gloss: Coming in or arriving.
examples: The phone blocks *incoming* calls from unknown numbers.
*Incoming* freshmen move in on Saturday.

senses.gloss: About to take over a job or an office from someone else.
examples: The *incoming* mayor takes office in January.
The *incoming* class of senators is unusually young.

contrast: The stress moves off *compare*: in-KAHM-pur-uh-buhl, not in-kum-PAIR-uh-buhl.

senses.gloss: So good that nothing else comes close.
examples: The view from the ridge is *incomparable*.
She was an *incomparable* teacher of young children.
His timing as a comedian is *incomparable*.

senses.gloss: Unable to work, exist or live together.
examples: The old printer is *incompatible* with this laptop.
They split up as an *incompatible* couple after two years.
The two accounts of the evening are more *incompatible* the closer you read them.

contrast: In law it also means unfit to stand trial or to manage your own affairs: *ruled mentally incompetent*.

senses.gloss: Not able to do a job properly.
examples: The contractor turned out to be completely *incompetent*.
An *incompetent* manager can ruin a good team.
He is the most *incompetent* driver I have ever ridden with.

contrast: In American schools an *incomplete* is also a noun: a grade that says the work is not finished yet.

senses.gloss: Missing a part, or not finished.
examples: The application is *incomplete* without a signature.
We have only *incomplete* records from before 1940.
His third pass of the night was *incomplete*.

senses.gloss: Impossible to understand.
examples: The instructions are *incomprehensible* to anyone but an engineer.
He left an *incomprehensible* voicemail at two in the morning.
Her decision to quit is *incomprehensible* to the rest of us.

senses.gloss: So unlikely or so strange that you cannot imagine it.
examples: It is *inconceivable* that nobody noticed the money was gone.
A phone without a camera seems *inconceivable* to my students.
Fifty years ago the idea was *inconceivable*.

senses.gloss: Not leading to a clear answer or result.
examples: The blood test came back *inconclusive*.
After three hours of *inconclusive* talks, they went home.
The second round of results was even more *inconclusive*.

senses.gloss: Out of place next to everything around it.
examples: A glass tower looks *incongruous* on that old street.
There was something *incongruous* about a tuxedo at a picnic.
Nothing could be more *incongruous* than palm trees in Ohio.

senses.gloss: Too small or minor to matter.
examples: We argued for an hour over something *inconsequential*.
The changes to the contract are *inconsequential*.
His objection was the most *inconsequential* of the three.

contrast: Not *inconsiderable*, a different word meaning small or not worth counting — usually met as the double negative *not inconsiderable* (= sizable).

senses.gloss: Not thinking about how your behavior affects other people.
examples: Playing music at 3 a.m. is *inconsiderate*.
It was *inconsiderate* of him to cancel an hour before dinner.
Our new neighbors are even more *inconsiderate* than the last ones.

senses.gloss: Changing from one time to the next; not steady.
examples: His work is good but *inconsistent*.
The team has been *inconsistent* all season.
Her sleep got more *inconsistent* after the baby arrived.

senses.gloss: Not matching something else, so that both cannot be true.
examples: His story is *inconsistent* with the security video.
The two reports are *inconsistent* on the date.

senses.gloss: So sad that nothing anyone says helps.
examples: She was *inconsolable* for weeks after the funeral.
The little boy was *inconsolable* when the dog died.
His *inconsolable* grief frightened the whole family.

senses.gloss: Not easy to notice.
examples: The entrance is small and *inconspicuous*.
He tried to make himself *inconspicuous* at the back of the room.
A gray car is more *inconspicuous* than a red one.

senses.gloss: So clear that nobody can argue against it.
examples: The DNA evidence is *incontestable*.
She has an *incontestable* claim to the land.
That he saved the company is *incontestable*.

form: in- + *continent* in its old sense *holding in*
contrast: Nothing to do with the noun *continent* (континент), though the two are spelled the same.

senses.gloss: Unable to control the bladder or bowels.
examples: After the stroke he was *incontinent* for several months.
The ward has special bedding for *incontinent* patients.
Many older dogs become *incontinent*.

senses.gloss: Impossible to deny or disprove.
examples: The prosecution called the fingerprints *incontrovertible*.
There is now *incontrovertible* proof that the emails were edited.
The link between smoking and cancer is *incontrovertible*.

senses.gloss: Causing trouble or extra effort, usually because of bad timing or a bad location.
examples: The meeting is at an *inconvenient* hour for the West Coast.
If Friday is *inconvenient* for you, we can move it.
They picked the most *inconvenient* week of the year to repave the street.

contrast: About behavior, English prefers *inappropriate*; *incorrect* is mostly about facts and answers.

senses.gloss: Wrong; not right or not accurate.
examples: Three of your answers are *incorrect*.
The address on the label was *incorrect*.
He gave an *incorrect* date for the meeting.

contrast: Often affectionate rather than harsh: *you are incorrigible* can be said with a laugh.

senses.gloss: Behaving badly in a way that cannot be changed.
examples: He is an *incorrigible* flirt.
Her son is *incorrigible* about leaving dishes in the sink.
The judge called him an *incorrigible* repeat offender.

senses.gloss: Impossible to bribe or to talk into doing something dishonest.
examples: The city needs an *incorruptible* inspector.
Everyone agreed the old judge was *incorruptible*.
He built a reputation as an *incorruptible* cop.

contrast: The verb *increase* is stressed in-KREESS; the noun is IN-kreess.

senses.gloss: Larger than before.
examples: Smokers face an *increased* risk of heart disease.
The bill gives schools *increased* funding for reading.
*Increased* demand pushed the price up.

senses.gloss: Getting bigger or more frequent.
examples: There is *increasing* pressure on the mayor to resign.
She spoke with *increasing* confidence as the year went on.
Wildfires arrive with *increasing* frequency.

contrast: *Incredible* describes the thing; *incredulous* describes the person who cannot believe it. A story is *incredible*, a listener is *incredulous*.

senses.gloss: Extremely good or impressive.
examples: The food at that place is *incredible*.
She did an *incredible* job on the presentation.
It was the most *incredible* week of my life.

senses.gloss: Too strange or extreme to believe.
examples: He told an *incredible* story about a bear in his kitchen.
The amount of trash they collected is *incredible*.

contrast: Not *incredible*: a person is *incredulous*, the news is *incredible*.

senses.gloss: Unable to believe what you are hearing or seeing.
examples: She gave me an *incredulous* look.
He was *incredulous* that anyone would pay that much for a bike.
The longer he talked, the more *incredulous* the jury became.

senses.gloss: Happening in small steps rather than all at once.
examples: The team made *incremental* improvements every week.
Reform here is *incremental*, never dramatic.
We saw an *incremental* gain of about two percent.

senses.gloss: Making someone look guilty of a crime.
examples: Police found *incriminating* text messages on his phone.
Nothing in the safe was *incriminating*.
The second video is far more *incriminating* than the first.

ru: действующий (о должностном лице); лежащий на ком-либо (об обязанности)
contrast: Also a noun: *the incumbent* is the person who currently holds the office.

senses.gloss: Currently holding an office or a job.
examples: The *incumbent* senator is running for a fourth term.
*Incumbent* mayors rarely lose in this city.

senses.gloss: Required of someone as a duty.
examples: It is *incumbent* on every driver to check the mirrors.
The court said it was *incumbent* upon the school to act.

senses.gloss: Impossible to cure.
examples: The disease is serious but not *incurable*.
He was treated for an *incurable* form of cancer.

senses.gloss: Having a habit or quality that will never change.
examples: My father is an *incurable* optimist.
She is an *incurable* romantic about old houses.

position: both — the *grateful* sense only after a verb

senses.gloss: Grateful to someone for their help.
examples: I am *indebted* to my sister for getting me through that year.
We remain *indebted* to the volunteers who stayed all night.
No one is more *indebted* to that teacher than I am.

senses.gloss: Owing a lot of money.
examples: The plan offers relief to heavily *indebted* countries.
Many graduates are deeply *indebted* before their first job.

contrast: In law, *indecent exposure* is a criminal charge. *Indecent haste* means offensively fast, not improper dress.

senses.gloss: Offensive, especially about sex or the body.
examples: He was arrested for *indecent* exposure.
The station was fined for broadcasting material far more *indecent* than that.
They remarried with what the neighbors called *indecent* haste.

senses.gloss: Impossible to read or to work out.
examples: The doctor's handwriting is *indecipherable*.
He left an *indecipherable* note on the counter.
Half the inscription is worn away and *indecipherable*.

senses.gloss: Unable to make up your mind.
examples: He is hopelessly *indecisive* in restaurants.
An *indecisive* manager slows the whole team down.
She gets more *indecisive* the more options you give her.

senses.gloss: Not settling anything.
examples: The battle was long and *indecisive*.
A second *indecisive* election forced a runoff.

form: in- + *defatigable*, from the Latin for *tire out*

senses.gloss: Never getting tired, however long the work goes on.
examples: She was an *indefatigable* campaigner for clean water.
His energy at eighty is *indefatigable*.
The paper owes the story to one *indefatigable* reporter.

senses.gloss: Impossible to excuse or to argue for.
examples: Hitting a child is *indefensible*.
The company made an *indefensible* decision to stay quiet.
His conduct that night was *indefensible*.

senses.gloss: Real, but impossible to put into words.
examples: The room had an *indefinable* smell of old paper.
There is an *indefinable* sadness in her early songs.
Something about the place is *indefinable* and hard to leave.

contrast: A grammar term as well: *a* and *an* are the *indefinite* articles.

senses.gloss: With no fixed end or limit.
examples: The store closed for an *indefinite* period.
He was put on *indefinite* leave after the complaint.

senses.gloss: Not clear or exact.
examples: Their plans for the summer are still *indefinite*.
She gave an *indefinite* answer about the money.

form: in- + a Latin root meaning *blot out*

senses.gloss: Impossible to wash off or remove.
examples: Label the boxes with an *indelible* marker.
The ink on ballots is *indelible* on purpose.

senses.gloss: Impossible to forget.
examples: That summer left an *indelible* impression on me.
The photograph is *indelible* once you have seen it.

senses.gloss: Slightly rude or embarrassing, especially in what you say.
examples: It would be *indelicate* to ask what she paid for it.
He made an *indelicate* joke at the reception.
Of all the questions, that was the most *indelicate*.

senses.gloss: Set in from the margin.
examples: Every quotation is *indented* half an inch.
The first line of each paragraph should be *indented*.

senses.gloss: With notches or deep cuts along the edge.
examples: Maine has a deeply *indented* coastline.
The leaf has an *indented* edge.

senses.gloss: Too extreme or too strange for words.
examples: The noise in the stadium was *indescribable*.
She felt an *indescribable* relief when the phone finally rang.
The smell of that market is *indescribable*.

senses.gloss: Impossible to break or destroy.
examples: The case is advertised as *indestructible*.
We bought an *indestructible* chew toy that lasted a week.
Their friendship seemed *indestructible*.

senses.gloss: Not exactly known or fixed.
examples: A man of *indeterminate* age answered the door.
The soup was an *indeterminate* shade of brown.
He got an *indeterminate* sentence of five to ten years.

senses.gloss: Provided with an index, or listed in one.
examples: The book is thoroughly *indexed*.
Older issues are not *indexed* online yet.

senses.gloss: Tied by a formula to prices, wages or another measure.
examples: Benefits are *indexed* to inflation.
They offered an *indexed* pension instead of a raise.

position: both — the *indicative of* sense only after a verb

senses.gloss: Showing or suggesting that something is true.
examples: A low turnout is *indicative* of how people feel about the race.
The rash is *indicative* of an allergy, not an infection.

senses.gloss: In grammar, the ordinary mood used for facts and questions.
examples: *She works here* is in the *indicative* mood.
Spanish learners meet the *indicative* long before the subjunctive.

contrast: Also a noun: *an indie* is an independent film, label or game studio.

senses.gloss: Made outside the big studios, labels or publishers.
examples: She writes for an *indie* magazine in Portland.
The theater shows *indie* films on Tuesdays.
His band started on a tiny *indie* label.

contrast: Not *different*. Also not the Russian «индифферентный» of chemistry — in everyday English it is about not caring.

senses.gloss: Not caring about something one way or the other.
examples: He seemed *indifferent* to the noise around him.
Voters are not hostile, just *indifferent*.
The longer the trial went on, the more *indifferent* the crowd became.

senses.gloss: Not very good; ordinary.
examples: We had an *indifferent* meal at a place near the station.
After an *indifferent* start, the team won nine in a row.

contrast: Capitalized when it refers to peoples: *Indigenous communities in Alaska*. Of plants and animals it stays lowercase.

senses.gloss: Originally from a particular place rather than brought there.
examples: These birds are *indigenous* to the islands.
The park is replanting *indigenous* grasses.
The museum was built with *Indigenous* leaders at the table.

contrast: Formal and mostly legal; in ordinary speech Americans say *poor* or *low-income*. Also a noun: *the indigent*.

senses.gloss: Too poor to pay for basic needs.
examples: The county provides a lawyer for *indigent* defendants.
The clinic treats patients who are *indigent* or uninsured.
*Indigent* families qualify for the fee waiver.

senses.gloss: Hard or impossible for the stomach to break down.
examples: Raw beans are *indigestible* and can make you sick.
The crust was cold and *indigestible* by then.

senses.gloss: Too dense or dull to take in.
examples: The manual is an *indigestible* block of small print.
He turned an *indigestible* report into two clear pages.

senses.gloss: Angry because something seems unfair or insulting.
examples: She was *indignant* at being asked to prove she worked there.
He sent an *indignant* letter to the editor.
The more they explained the fee, the more *indignant* he got.

contrast: Also a noun for the dye and the color: *dyed with indigo*.

senses.gloss: Deep blue with a hint of violet.
examples: She wore an *indigo* dress to the wedding.
The sky over the desert turned *indigo*.
They still dye the cloth *indigo* by hand.

contrast: A grammar term as well: *indirect speech* and *indirect questions* keep statement word order — *He asked where I lived*.

senses.gloss: Not going straight from one point to another.
examples: We took an *indirect* route to avoid the bridge.
The flight was cheap but *indirect*.

senses.gloss: Not the immediate cause, or not said openly.
examples: Stress was an *indirect* cause of his illness.
She has an *indirect* way of saying no.
His criticism was more *indirect* this time.

senses.gloss: Too faint or too slight to be made out.
examples: The difference in taste was *indiscernible*.
At that distance the marks are *indiscernible*.
The copy is *indiscernible* from the original.

contrast: Two traps in one word: *discreet* (tactful) is not *discrete* (separate), and *indiscreet* is not *indiscrete*.

senses.gloss: Saying or doing something that should have been kept private.
examples: One *indiscreet* remark cost him the job.
It was *indiscreet* of her to forward that email.
He gets more *indiscreet* after a second glass of wine.

form: in- + *discriminate*, in its old sense *tell apart*

senses.gloss: Done without care about who or what is affected.
examples: The report condemns the *indiscriminate* shelling of villages.
*Indiscriminate* use of antibiotics breeds resistant bacteria.
His reading is wide but *indiscriminate*.

senses.gloss: So necessary that you could not manage without it.
examples: A good dictionary is *indispensable* for translation work.
She made herself *indispensable* in her first year.
The truck is *indispensable* to the business.

contrast: Formal and often a polite cover story: *she is indisposed* can mean anything from a headache to not wanting to come.

senses.gloss: Slightly ill.
examples: The senator is *indisposed* and will not speak today.
He was *indisposed* all weekend with a stomach bug.

senses.gloss: Not willing to do something.
examples: The bank seems *indisposed* to lend on those terms.
She was *indisposed* to discuss it any further.

senses.gloss: So certain that no one can argue with it.
examples: Her talent is *indisputable*.
The report lays out the *indisputable* facts first.
It is *indisputable* that the bridge needs work.

senses.gloss: Hard to see, hear or remember clearly.
examples: The shapes in the fog were *indistinct*.
His voice on the tape is *indistinct*.
My memory of that day gets more *indistinct* every year.

senses.gloss: So alike that you cannot tell one from the other.
examples: The fake is *indistinguishable* from the real bill.
The twins were *indistinguishable* in their school photos.
At that speed the spokes become an *indistinguishable* blur.

contrast: Very common as a noun too: *an individual* is a single person — *three individuals were questioned*.

senses.gloss: Single and separate, considered one at a time.
examples: Each *individual* student meets with the adviser once.
The cookies come in *individual* wrappers.

senses.gloss: Belonging to or designed for one person.
examples: Teachers here give a lot of *individual* attention.
The gym writes an *individual* plan for every member.

senses.gloss: Putting the single person ahead of the group, or doing things your own way.
examples: American culture is often called *individualistic*.
He has an *individualistic* style that the coach tolerates.
The younger players are more *individualistic* than the old team was.

contrast: American spelling keeps *-ized*; British writing often has *individualised*.

senses.gloss: Shaped to fit one particular person.
examples: Every student on the plan gets an *individualized* reading list.
The clinic offers *individualized* treatment rather than one protocol.
Their training is *individualized* down to the week.

senses.gloss: Impossible to divide or separate into parts.
examples: The pledge calls the nation *indivisible*.
Seven is *indivisible* by two.
For her, work and family form one *indivisible* whole.

contrast: Literary; in speech Americans say *lazy*. In medicine an *indolent* tumor is one that grows slowly.

senses.gloss: Lazy, in a comfortable and unhurried way.
examples: They spent an *indolent* afternoon by the lake.
The novel follows an *indolent* young man with too much money.
August makes the whole town more *indolent*.

senses.gloss: Impossible to defeat or discourage.
examples: She faced the diagnosis with *indomitable* good humor.
The team's *indomitable* spirit kept the season alive.
At ninety his will was still *indomitable*.

contrast: Formal and slightly old-fashioned; the adverb *indubitably* is more often met, usually as a joke.

senses.gloss: Not open to any doubt.
examples: The letters are of *indubitable* importance to historians.
He is an *indubitable* master of the short story.
Her right to the money is *indubitable*.
